content.p: In the first week of October 1967, federal soldiers fighting Biafran secessionists in Nigeria's civil war took the town of Asaba, on the western bank of the River Niger, and killed a large number of its men and boys. The worst of it came on 7 October. Townspeople had been told to gather and show their loyalty, and many came out in white ceremonial dress, singing and chanting "One Nigeria". The men and older boys were separated from the women and young children and shot in an open square.

The dead were buried in pits where they fell. Nobody issued death certificates, and no government counted them. The scholars who studied the killings most closely put the toll at 500 to 800; Nigerian newspapers and the town's memorial committee say it exceeded 1,000. Fifty-nine years later the argument over the number, over who gave the order, and over whether Nigeria's government has ever properly apologised is still open.
content.h2: A town west of the river
content.p: Asaba faces the city of Onitsha across the Niger. The two are close, but they sat on different sides of the war. Asaba's people are ethnically and linguistically Igbo, according to the memorial monument project, yet the town was never part of Biafra, the breakaway state that Colonel Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu proclaimed on 30 May 1967 after the federal government carved the old regions into twelve states. Vanguard notes that the people of Asaba usually call themselves Anioma. The University of South Florida's account adds that earlier massacres of Igbo people elsewhere in Nigeria had already driven many Igbo to flee south, mostly toward Delta State.

In August 1967 Biafran troops crossed into the Mid-Western Region and took Benin City. Federal forces of the Second Division, under Colonel Murtala Muhammed, drove them back to the Niger. The retreating Biafrans crossed to Onitsha and blew up part of the bridge behind them, which stopped the federal troops from following. Vanguard's retelling suggests the soldiers may have been frustrated by that, and that they came into Asaba around 5 October claiming that the townsmen were Biafran sympathisers. The Centre for Nigeria Progress describes the atmosphere as one charged by suspicion of the town's Igbo ties and by the earlier pogroms in the north.

Vanguard also reports that the local Biafran commander, Colonel Joe Achizia, himself from Asaba, chose to retreat to Onitsha, and that the only equipment he was given to defend it was a lorry load of cutlasses.

On 5 and 6 October, according to the Centre for Nigeria Progress, soldiers ransacked and looted houses and killed men and boys they accused of being Biafran fighters or collaborators, singly and in small groups, at places including the area of a police station and a football field. Vanguard says hundreds may have died in this first phase.

Fearing worse, community leaders called the people out on the morning of 7 October. The Centre for Nigeria Progress says town criers summoned residents from Asaba's five quarters, and that the crowd paraded down Nnebisi Road. Vanguard reports that hundreds of men, women and children, most in white akwa ocha, sang, danced and chanted for "One Nigeria". The aim, as Vanguard puts it, was to end the violence by a show of unity.

At a junction the soldiers divided the crowd. Men and teenage boys were held back and taken to an open square at Ogbe-Osowa, while women and young children were sent elsewhere. Machine guns were brought out, and orders to fire were given. Vanguard and the Centre for Nigeria Progress both name Major Ibrahim Taiwo, the division's second in command, as the officer reported to have given that order. The Sun says the order was "reportedly" given by him, and the Centre for Nigeria Progress calls him "frequently cited" in accounts. These are reports, not a court finding.

Chiedu "Cassy" Juwah was about ten at the time. Vanguard quotes his recollection of a welcome party at the Ogbe-Ilo field that soldiers broke up. On the 7th, he said, he and others were rounded up and herded to Oma, where they were divided; he, being a boy, went with the women to a convent, now St John Bosco's Church, while Ogbe-Osowa "became a killing field". His brother Augustine, he said, pretended to be dead among the bodies, and by 8 p.m. had made his way home. People then fled, first to Achala and then to Ubulu-Uku. Some who came back days later, Juwah said, were killed in house-to-house searches.

Professor Emmanuel Nwanze, a former vice-chancellor of the University of Benin, said in a lecture quoted by Vanguard that the men "naively complied" when told to separate by sex, because nothing like it had happened to them before. When the shooting stopped, he said, the groans of the dying could be heard, and some of the half-dead who had been knocked down by falling bodies called to the soldiers to finish the job.

No official count exists. The University of South Florida's account says lists of many of the dead exist, but families could not bury their men one by one as custom demands, and no certificates were written. Survivors buried the dead in pits on the site.

The figures differ. The Asaba Development Council compiled a list of 373 named victims in 1981 and acknowledged it as incomplete, according to the Centre for Nigeria Progress. The same article gives 500 to 800 as the range of Bird and Ottanelli, who interviewed more than 100 survivors, military figures and officials and used archives for their 2017 book. The University of South Florida says 500 to 700 were killed, most in the Ogbe-Osowa square. Vanguard's 2020 report says over 700 men and boys died in the square, some aged 12, and that the total for early October was over 1,000, although "the exact numbers were likely not known". Another Vanguard column puts the three days at about 1,000 and adds that more died later in the bush from hunger, wounds or capture. The Asaba Massacre Memorial Monument project also says an estimated 1,000 men and boys died.

The writer Rudolf Okonkwo, in Gazette Nigeria, says the soldiers killed more people in the days after the main shooting. Vanguard's columnist goes further and says killing spilled into other towns of the Anioma area, claiming that troops killed 400 people one night in the coastal village of Ishiagwu. That figure comes from a single opinion piece, not from an official record.

The killing did not end the ordeal. According to Vanguard, many extended families lost dozens of men and boys, and the soldiers occupied Asaba for months, during which most parts of the town were destroyed and many women and girls were raped or forcibly "married". Many people fled and did not come back until the war ended in 1970. The Centre for Nigeria Progress adds that a second operation in April 1968, after a brief Biafran incursion, brought more roundups and killings and that St Patrick's College served as a refugee camp. Chike Osadebey, son of the former Mid-Western premier Dennis Osadebey, told the Sun that nearly every family in the closely knit town had a victim, and that he lost uncles, aunts and cousins.

OldNaija records one of the survivors on film, Patience Chukwura, who was then a young mother expecting her fourth child; she said her husband, Eddie, was killed, along with her father-in-law and two brothers-in-law.

Several explanations are offered, none settled. The Sun says it was alleged that the massacre was meant to teach the Mid-Western region a lesson for sympathising with Biafrans. Writing in Gazette Nigeria, Okonkwo says the book by Bird and Ottanelli shows a different motive: that Asaba was the home area of soldiers connected to Major Kaduna Nzeogwu, who led the January 1966 coup, whose parents came from Okpanam, a few kilometres away. A witness quoted by the Sun, Dr Cyril Gwam, made a similar claim, saying the troops thought they were killing relatives of Nzeogwu and were on a revenge mission, not hunting Biafrans. Okonkwo quotes a government official interviewed in the book describing Murtala Muhammed as "fairly tempestuous". Those are accounts and interpretations, not judicial findings.

For years the killings were hardly mentioned. Vanguard says Bill Norris of the London Times passed through Asaba in mid-October 1967 and sent photographs of ruin and abandonment but said nothing of a massacre; in a 2012 interview he said he did not know about it. The first published mention, in the London Observer almost four months later, came from the Africa correspondent Colin Legum, who confirmed that federal troops took part. His second-hand account said a group of "implacably hostile" Igbo had surprised the soldiers during the welcome dance and that the killing was retaliation, according to Vanguard.
content.h2: The Oputa Panel and Gowon's apology
content.p: In 2001 some survivors told their stories to the Human Rights Violations Investigation Commission, called the Oputa Panel after its chair. The University of South Florida stresses that, unlike truth commissions in South Africa and elsewhere, it was not designed to assign blame or to act.

Major General Ibrahim Haruna also appeared. Gazette Nigeria quotes him describing himself as the commanding officer of troops that, in the quoted words, massacred 500 men in Asaba, and saying he had no apology for the dead. "I acted as a soldier maintaining the peace and unity of Nigeria," he is quoted as saying. Some historians dispute that he was in Asaba at all in 1967, the same article notes, and Vanguard says he took over the Second Division from Murtala Muhammed only in 1968. Vanguard adds that no eyewitness report has Muhammed himself giving the order, but that, as field commander, he should take responsibility, in that column's view.

Yakubu Gowon, head of state during the war, apologised to the people of Asaba in September 2001, according to the University of South Florida. In December 2002, speaking in Asaba at a national prayer rally, he repeated it. A newspaper report of that day, preserved by the university, quotes him saying that he felt touched, asked forgiveness "being the one who was in charge that time", and said the killings were "not something that I would have approved of". He said he was made ignorant of it until it appeared in the papers. He spoke, he said, on behalf of himself and the government of Nigeria at the time.

The monument project's website nevertheless says that no official apology or explanation has been offered by the federal government. These two statements can be read together: Gowon spoke as a former leader, not as a sitting one.
content.h2: Memory, memorials and calls for redress
content.p: In October 2017 Asaba marked the 50th anniversary with a two-day commemoration themed "In Pursuit of Rebirth", and Bird and Ottanelli's book on the killings, published by Cambridge University Press, was launched. Vanguard's report lists guests including the Nobel laureate Wole Soyinka, former vice president Alex Ekwueme and Delta State's governor, Ifeanyi Okowa. Soyinka said restitution was "the capstone" of healing and objected to streets and public works named after men he blamed for grave crimes. Other speakers asked the federal government for a memorial plaque bearing the victims' names at Ogbe-Osowa.

The Asaba Massacre Memorial Monument project now plans a memorial park, and the Asaba Memorial Project at the University of South Florida works with the town to document the history. The monument project's website calls the massacre one of the most underreported atrocities of the 20th century.

On 7 October 2025, the 58th anniversary, the Asagba of Asaba, Professor Epiphany Azinge, led thousands in a minute of silence at noon. The Guardian Nigeria reports that he asked President Bola Tinubu for a presidential apology and a federal university in Asaba in the victims' memory. The Isama Ajie of Asaba, Chief Chuck Nduka-Eze, announced that the silence would be repeated every 7 October at noon with a 21-gun salute, and that the president, when the town raised its concerns with him, had been silent on the massacre.
